Hussain-lab-05

Part 1: Configuring my project and examining the data

The NMES1988 data describe 4,406 adults aged 66 and older from the 1987–1988 US National Medical Expenditure Survey. It details several variables with the outcome variable being number of physician office visits. The rest are listed below

Variable Description
visits Outcome: physician office visits between 1987 and 1988
chronic Number of chronic conditions
health Self-perceived health: poor, average, or excellent
gender male of female
school Years of education
insurance Covered by private insurance: no or yes

Reference groups are Average health, Male, and No insurance.

n mean var p_zero max
4406 5.774399 45.68712 0.1550159 89

The visits outcome is a count. Whole numbers, bounded at zero, and right-skewed. The variance (45.69) is about 7.91 times the mean (5.77). 16% of people had no visits. The greatest number of visits reported (89)is a shockingly large number, but could be legitimate.

Part 2: Specifying competing count models

A linear model is a poor choice for the visits outcome variable because the visits data are counts, meaning that negative visits and half visits are impossible/meaningless values. This is evidenced by the DHARMa simulations. The residuals, shown in the QQ plot, do not follow the expected flat diagonal line. The outlier and KS tests also speak to this concern. In the residual-vs-predicted plot, as the predicted probability approaches 1, the distribution becomes more compressed toward the lower end of residual values. This is also evidenced by the red 0.5 quantile line. Taken together, its clear these data are not a good fit for a Gaussian model.

Model AIC BIC Log-likelihood Deviance Residual.df Nested df Nested χ² Nested p
M0: Null 39,720.340 39,726.731 −19,859.170 26,942.921 4405 — — —
M1: Chronic_pred 37,546.913 37,559.694 −18,771.456 24,767.493 4404 1 2,175.428 < .001
M2: Full 36,596.989 36,641.724 −18,291.494 23,807.569 4399 5 959.924 < .001

For the comparison between M0 and M1, nested χ² = 2,175.428, p <.001. For the comparison between M1 and M2, nested χ² = 959.924, p <.001. Both of these likelihood-ratio tests indicate a statistically significant improvement in model fit. This means that adding the additional predictors improved the model fit across both comparisons, suggesting that M2 is a better fit model than M1 and M0. Further, the AIC and BIC decreased for both comparisons, once again implying that M2 is a good model to select. For these reasons, I have selected M2 as the ideal model.

Part 3: Evaluating the Poisson model

The provisionally selected model is M2: Full.

Its performance is:

  • AIC = 3.6596989^{4}
  • BIC = 3.6641724^{4}

    DHARMa nonparametric dispersion test via sd of residuals fitted vs.
    simulated

data:  simulationOutput
dispersion = 7.2521, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

    DHARMa zero-inflation test via comparison to expected zeros with
    simulation under H0 = fitted model

data:  simulationOutput
ratioObsSim = 15.035, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

The DHARMa plots suggest that the Poisson model is a poor fit. The dispersion ratio is 7.25 (p < .001), and there are 15.03 times as many zeros as the Poisson expects. The observed data are more variable than a Poisson allows.

The over dispersion observed here matters because it means that the assumption that the variance is equal to the mean has been violated. In this case the variance is underestimated, meaning that model’s standard errors are too small, the confidence intervals are too narrow, and the p-values are too small. I would not move straight to a zero-inflated model based on this zero-inflation test alone because the test only tells me that there are more zeros than the Poisson expects, it does not tell me if these zeros are coming from structural reasons (i.e. some people have no reason to visit a doctor during this period). Whether the zeros are structural or not will define if I should move to a zero-inflated model.

The negative binomial model fit significantly better than the full Poisson model, χ²(1) = 1.212908^{4}, p < .001.

This test has 1 degree of freedom because the negative binomial model adds more more layer of complexity by adding one parameter that describes the extra variability in the data. Yes, the NB2 fit significantly better than the Poisson. This is evidenced by the large reduction in AIC and BIC and the significance of the LRT test. This tells us that adding complexity to the model didn’t take away from the significance of the relationship. The NB2 resolved our over dispersion issue, but our issue of excess zero may remain.

The NB resolved the over dispersion: the dispersion ratio is now 1.04 (p = 0.432), close to 1 and non-significant.

The line curves upward even though the model is linear in its predictors because of the the log link: each additional chronic condition adds a constant amount on the log scale, multiplying the expected count, so the same one-condition increase adds more visits when the expected count is already high.

Part 5: Do the zeros need their own model?

Given that my NB2 zero-inflation test produced a significant result, I will test ZINB and Hurdle NB models to see if the fit is improved and the zero-inflation is resolved.

data:  simulationOutput

I will carry forward the hurdle negative binomial model for a few reasons. Initially, the ZINB-full model was found to fit significantly better than the ordinary negative binomial model. This was a good first step of providing evidence that adding the zero-inflation component improves the model.The DHARMa result for the ZINB-full model was ratioObsSim = 0.95671, p = 0.176. The p being > .05, indicated there was no statistically significant evidence of remaining zero inflation. I then conducted the same test for the hurdle model and found that the results were ratioObsSim = 0.99928, p = 1. Since p > .05 again, this meant that there was no statistically significant evidence of remaining zero inflation for the hurdle model either. Because both the ZINB-full and hurdle models passed the DHARMa zero-inflation test, the decision for which model to select is now based on the AIC/BIC comparison of the two model options. The comparison showed that the hurdle model had the lowest AIC (24,330.41) and BIC (24,426.27) of all four models. Thus, I choose to carry forward the hurdle model.

Part 6: Testing and probing an interaction

Question: Does the association between the number of chronic conditions and physician visits differ for people based on gender?

I predict that the association between number of chronic conditions and physician visits differs for male and female patients such that female patients will have a weaker association between the predictor and the outcome variable. My thinking here is that female health is not well understood in many domains, so while a female patients may be attending many visits to the doctor, they may not be able to report an accurate number of chronic conditions due to the fact that physicians may not provide adequate diagnoses. This would probably be especially true for female patients in the window of time we are examining (1987–1988).

The association between chronic conditions and visits is positive and significant for both genders.The p-value of .924 means that the two slopes do not significantly differ. The sign might be flipped because of the order of the subtraction. Since we only have two level for gender. If i called female - male instead, the sign would be positive. The two tests answer the same question with a two-level moderator because there is only one difference between the slopes that we can determine. The emmeans predicted counts differ slightly from the ggeffects plot, and the contrasts do not because they use different methods, but ultimately the difference remains the same despite the absolute predictions differing.

Simple Effects of Gender Across Chronic Conditions

Log contrasts = Male − Female. z-tests and p-values are computed on the log scale.

My hypothesis was not supported. There was no evidence that the association between the number of chronic conditions and physician visits differed between male and female patients. The likelihood-ratio test indicated that adding the chronic conditions × gender interaction did not significantly improve model fit, χ²(1) = 0.009, p = .924. Chronic conditions were positively associated with physician visits for both males (b = 0.194, p < .001) and females (b = 0.197, p < .001), but the difference between these slopes was not significant (p = .924). Simple-effects comparisons indicated that females had significantly higher predicted physician visit counts than males but, these gender differences did not significantly vary with the number of chronic conditions. So, I am not very confident in this interaction since neither the omnibus nor the probing supported my hypothesis.

Part 7: My findings

Write an APA-style results section in three paragraphs. Use inline R code.

Paragraph 1: Model selection. Describe the outcome and how you arrived at your final model. Report: • The mean, variance, and percentage of zeros for the outcome. • The Poisson model’s DHARMa dispersion ratio and zero-inflation ratio, with p-values. • The LRT comparing the Poisson and NB2 (χ², df, p). • The NB2’s dispersion and zero-inflation ratios, with p-values, and whether a separate model for the zeros was needed.

Paragraph 2: Main effects. Report the results of your selected model. For each predictor, give: • The coefficient (b), 95% CI, and p-value. • A plain-language interpretation of the direction of the association (e.g., “women published fewer articles than men”). State what is held constant, and identify which predictors were not significant.

Paragraph 3: Interaction. Report: • The LRT comparing the additive and interaction models (χ², df, p). • The simple slopes of chronic within each level of predictor2 (b, 95% CI, p). • The simple effects of predictor2 at −1 SD, the mean, and +1 SD of chronic (log contrast, p).

Summarize the overall pattern in one sentence. For example, where is the difference between groups largest, and where does it disappear?

7.2. Discussion What do your results suggest about the relative importance of chronic conditions, self-perceived health, or other variables regarding how often older adults visit a physician? What are the main limitations of this analysis?

example

Article counts were overdispersed (M = 1.69, s² = 3.71; 30% zeros). Simulation-based residual checks on a Poisson model showed significant overdispersion (dispersion ratio = 1.99, p < .001) and excess zeros (observed/expected = 1.44, p < .001). A negative binomial model fit significantly better, χ²(1) = 180.20, p < .001, and showed no remaining evidence of overdispersion (ratio = 1.05, p = .556) or excess zeros (ratio = 0.99, p = .772), so no separate model for zeros was needed.

Holding other predictors constant, women published fewer articles than men (b = −0.22, 95% CI [−0.36, −0.07], p = .003). Each additional child aged 5 or younger was associated with fewer articles (b = −0.18, 95% CI [−0.28, −0.07], p < .001), and each additional mentor article with more articles (b = 0.029, 95% CI [0.023, 0.035], p < .001). Marital status (b = 0.15, 95% CI [−0.01, 0.31], p = .067) and PhD prestige (b = 0.02, 95% CI [−0.06, 0.09], p = .672) were not significantly associated with article counts.

Adding a PhD prestige × gender interaction did not significantly improve fit, χ²(1) = 3.73, p = .053. Simple slopes showed that prestige was not significantly associated with article counts for men (b = −0.04, 95% CI [−0.14, 0.05], p = .363) or women (b = 0.10, 95% CI [−0.01, 0.20], p = .084). Simple effects, however, showed that the gender gap narrowed as prestige increased. Men were expected to publish more articles than women at low prestige (−1 SD; b = 0.36, p < .001) and at average prestige (b = 0.22, p = .002), but the difference was not significant at high prestige (+1 SD; b = 0.09, p = .354).

# Part 1: Configuring my project and examining the data

```{r, set up}
#| echo: FALSE

library(tidyverse)
library(glmmTMB)
library(DHARMa)
library(ggeffects)
library(emmeans)
library(performance)
library(broom.mixed)
library(gt)
library(AER)

```

```{r, dataset setup}
#| echo: FALSE

# Data loading

data("NMES1988")

data <- NMES1988

# Selecting my variables of interest 

data <- data |>
  select(visits, chronic, health, gender, school, insurance) |> 

#Assigning reference groups of Men and Single
  
  mutate(
    health = fct_relevel(factor(health), "average"),
    gender = fct_relevel(factor(gender), "male"),
    insurance = fct_relevel(factor(insurance), "no")
  )

```

The `NMES1988` data describe 4,406 adults aged 66 and older from the 1987–1988 US National Medical Expenditure Survey. It details several variables with the outcome variable being number of physician office visits. The rest are listed below

| Variable    | Description                                                |
|-------------|------------------------------------------------------------|
| `visits`    | **Outcome:** physician office visits between 1987 and 1988 |
| `chronic`   | Number of chronic conditions                               |
| `health`    | Self-perceived health: `poor`, `average`, or `excellent`   |
| `gender`    | `male` of `female`                                         |
| `school`    | Years of education                                         |
| `insurance` | Covered by private insurance: `no` or `yes`                |

Reference groups are **Average** health, **Male**, and **No** insurance.


```{r describe}
#| echo: FALSE

# Describe the data

visits_summary <- data |>
  summarise(
    n      = n(),
    mean   = mean(visits),
    var    = var(visits),
    p_zero = mean(visits == 0),
    max    = max(visits)
  )

# making it a proper table
gt(visits_summary)

```

```{r descriptive plot}
#| echo: FALSE

# Creating a plot of the overall distribution of the outcome variable (number of visits)
descriptive_plot <- ggplot(data, aes(x = visits)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Number of visits", y = "Number of People")

descriptive_plot

```

The visits outcome **is a count.** Whole numbers, bounded at zero, and right-skewed. **The variance (`r round(visits_summary$var, 2)`) is about `r round(visits_summary$var / visits_summary$mean, 2)` times the mean (`r round(visits_summary$mean, 2)`).** **`r round(100 * visits_summary$p_zero)`% of people had no visits.** The greatest number of visits reported **(`r round(visits_summary$max, 2)`)**is a shockingly large number, but could be legitimate. 

# Part 2: Specifying competing count models

```{r, gaussian model test}
#| echo: FALSE

# Fitting a Gaussian model

m_gauss <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data,
  family = gaussian(link = "identity")
)

#simulation 
set.seed(500)
res_gauss <- simulateResiduals(m_gauss, n = 500, plot = FALSE)
plot(res_gauss)

```


A linear model is a poor choice for the visits outcome variable because the visits data are counts, meaning that negative visits and half visits are impossible/meaningless values. This is evidenced by the DHARMa simulations. The residuals, shown in the QQ plot, do not follow the expected flat diagonal line. The outlier and KS tests also speak to this concern. In the residual-vs-predicted plot, as the predicted probability approaches 1, the distribution becomes more compressed toward the lower end of residual values. This is also evidenced by the red 0.5 quantile line. Taken together, its clear these data are not a good fit for a Gaussian model. 


```{r poisson null}
#| echo: FALSE

# Null (intercept-only) Poisson model: no predictors
null <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ 1, 
  data = data, 
  family = poisson(link = "log"))

# One-predictor Poisson model: Does having a chronic condition predict visit counts?
chronic_pred <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic, 
  data = data, 
  family = poisson(link = "log"))


# Full Poisson model: all five predictors at once. Chronic, health, gender, school, insurance explain additional variation. 
full <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data,
  family = poisson(link = "log"))

```


```{r, anova tests}
#| echo: FALSE

tests <- anova(null, chronic_pred, full)

```

```{r, prepare tests}
#| echo: FALSE

tests <- tests |>
  select(Chisq, `Chi Df`, `Pr(>Chisq)`) |>
  rename(
    Nested.df = `Chi Df`,
    Nested.Chisq.stat = Chisq,
    Nested.p.value = `Pr(>Chisq)`)

```

```{r, extract model metrics}
#| echo: FALSE

glance0 <- broom.mixed::glance(null)
glance1 <- broom.mixed::glance(chronic_pred)
glance2 <- broom.mixed::glance(full)

```

```{r, combine model metrics}
#| echo: FALSE

mods <- c(
  "M0: Null",
  "M1: Chronic_pred",
  "M2: Full")

glances <- rbind(
  glance0,
  glance1,
  glance2)
```

```{r, combine comparisons}
#| echo: FALSE

comparison_table <- cbind(
  Model = mods,
  glances,
  tests)

```

```{r, model comparison table}
#| echo: FALSE

comparison_table |>
  select(
    Model,
    AIC,
    BIC,
    logLik,
    deviance,
    df.residual,
    Nested.df,
    Nested.Chisq.stat,
    Nested.p.value
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    Model = "Model",
    AIC = "AIC",
    BIC = "BIC",
    logLik = "Log-likelihood",
    deviance = "Deviance",
    df.residual = "Residual.df",
    Nested.df = "Nested df",
    Nested.Chisq.stat = "Nested χ²",
    Nested.p.value = "Nested p"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      AIC,
      BIC,
      logLik,
      deviance,
      Nested.Chisq.stat
    ),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  fmt(
    columns = Nested.p.value,
    fns = function(x) {
      ifelse(
        is.na(x),
        "—",
        ifelse(x < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", x))
      )
    }
  ) |>
  sub_missing(
    columns = c(Nested.df, Nested.Chisq.stat),
    missing_text = "—"
  )

```

For the comparison between M0 and M1, nested χ² = 2,175.428, p <.001. For the comparison between M1 and M2, nested χ² = 959.924, p <.001. Both of these likelihood-ratio tests indicate a statistically significant improvement in model fit. This means that adding the additional predictors improved the model fit across both comparisons, suggesting that M2 is a better fit model than M1 and M0. Further, the AIC and BIC decreased for both comparisons, once again implying that M2 is a good model to select. For these reasons, I have selected M2 as the ideal model.  

# Part 3: Evaluating the Poisson model

```{r, select model}
#| echo: FALSE

selected_row <- comparison_table |>
  filter(Nested.p.value < .05) |>
  slice_tail(n = 1)

#creating an object with our selected model's name for dynamic reporting
selected_name <- selected_row$Model

#case matching for dynamic reporting
selected_model <- switch(
  selected_name,
  "M0: Null" = null,
  "M1: Chronic_pred" = chronic_pred,
  "M2: Full" = full,
  )

```

The provisionally selected model is **`r selected_name`**.

Its performance is:

- AIC = **`r round(AIC(selected_model), 3)`**
- BIC = **`r round(BIC(selected_model), 3)`**

```{r poisson dharma}
#| echo: FALSE

# Seed was always set to 500 for this whole document. 
set.seed(500)

# Simulates 500 new datasets from the fitted full poisson model.
res_pois <- simulateResiduals(full, n = 500, plot = FALSE)

#  QQ plot and residuals vs. predicted values
plot(res_pois)

```
```{r, pois-dispersion}
#| echo: FALSE

# Dispersion test

disp_pois <- testDispersion(res_pois)
disp_pois

```

```{r, poisson zeros}
#| echo: FALSE

# Zero-inflation test

zi_pois <- testZeroInflation(res_pois)
zi_pois

```


The DHARMa plots suggest that the Poisson model is a poor fit. The dispersion ratio is `r round(disp_pois$statistic, 2)` (`r ifelse(disp_pois$p.value < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(disp_pois$p.value, 3)))`), and there are `r round(zi_pois$statistic, 2)` times as many zeros as the Poisson expects. The observed data are more variable than a Poisson allows. 

The over dispersion observed here matters because it means that the assumption that the variance is equal to the mean has been violated. In this case the variance is underestimated, meaning that model's standard errors are too small, the confidence intervals are too narrow, and the *p*-values are too small. I would not move straight to a zero-inflated model based on this zero-inflation test alone because the test only tells me that there are more zeros than the Poisson expects, it does not tell me if these zeros are coming from structural reasons (i.e. some people have no reason to visit a doctor during this period). Whether the zeros are structural or not will define if I should move to a  zero-inflated model. 

# Part 4: Fitting and evaluating a negative binomial model

```{r, nb}
#| echo: FALSE

# Negative binomial (NB2) model
neg_binom <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data   = data,
  family = nbinom2(link = "log")
)

summary(neg_binom)

# LRT
lrt_nb<-anova(full, neg_binom)
lrt_nb

```

The negative binomial model fit significantly better than the full Poisson model, χ²(`r lrt_nb[2, "Chi Df"]`) = `r round(lrt_nb[2, "Chisq"], 2)`, `r ifelse(lrt_nb[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"] < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(lrt_nb[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"], 3)))`.

This test has 1 degree of freedom because the negative binomial model adds more more layer of complexity by adding one parameter that describes the extra variability in the data. Yes, the  NB2 fit significantly better than the Poisson. This is evidenced by the large reduction in AIC and BIC and the significance of the LRT test. This tells us that adding complexity to the model didn't take away from the significance of the relationship. The NB2 resolved our over dispersion issue, but our issue of excess zero may remain. 


```{r, nb-dharma}
#| echo: FALSE

# Same seed as before

set.seed(500)

# If the NB is adequate, these should now be uniform, unlike the Poisson's.
res_nb <- simulateResiduals(neg_binom, n = 500, plot = FALSE)

# QQ plot: points should now sit close to the diagonal.
# Residuals vs. predicted: should be roughly flat.
plot(res_nb)

```

```{r, nb-tests}
#| echo: FALSE

disp_nb <- testDispersion(res_nb)

# Zero inflation
zi_nb <- testZeroInflation(res_nb)

```

The NB resolved the over dispersion: the dispersion ratio is now `r round(disp_nb$statistic, 2)` (`r ifelse(disp_nb$p.value < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", round(disp_nb$p.value, 3)))`), close to 1 and non-significant.

```{r nb-pred-plot}
#| echo: FALSE

# Predicted mean visit counts from the additive NB, on the count scale.
# "chronic [0:20]" plots chronic conditions from 0 to 20.

pred_nb <- predict_response(neg_binom, terms = "chronic [0:20]")

plot(pred_nb) +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted visit counts by number of chronic conditions",
    x     = "Chronic conditions", y = "Predicted visits"
  )

```

The line curves upward even though the model is linear in its predictors because of the the log link: each additional chronic condition adds a constant amount on the log scale, multiplying the expected count, so the same one-condition increase adds more visits when the expected count is already high.

# Part 5: Do the zeros need their own model?

Given that my NB2 zero-inflation test produced a significant result, I will test ZINB
and Hurdle NB models to see if the fit is improved and the zero-inflation is resolved. 


```{r zero-models}
#| echo: FALSE

# Zero-inflated NB with a constant zero-inflation probability
m_zinb <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  ziformula = ~ 1,
  data = data, family = nbinom2()
)

# Zero-inflated NB with predictors in the zero part
m_zinb_full <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  ziformula = ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data, family = nbinom2()
)

# Hurdle NB
m_hurd <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  ziformula = ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data, family = truncated_nbinom2()
)

# Compare models
anova(neg_binom, m_zinb_full)

# The hurdle isn't nested in the NB, so compare with AIC/BIC (lower = better)
AIC(neg_binom, m_zinb, m_zinb_full, m_hurd)
BIC(neg_binom, m_zinb, m_zinb_full, m_hurd)

# Then re-check the chosen model with DHARMa - for zinb_full
set.seed(500)
res_zinb <- simulateResiduals(m_zinb_full, n = 500, plot = FALSE)
testZeroInflation(res_zinb)

# Then re-check the chosen model with DHARMa - this time for the hurdle model
set.seed(500)
res_hurd <- simulateResiduals(m_hurd, n = 500, plot = FALSE)
testZeroInflation(res_hurd)

```

I will carry forward the hurdle negative binomial model for a few reasons. Initially, the ZINB-full model was found to fit significantly better than the ordinary negative binomial model. This was a good first step of providing evidence that adding the zero-inflation component improves the model.The DHARMa result for the ZINB-full model was ratioObsSim = 0.95671, p = 0.176. The p being > .05, indicated there was no statistically significant evidence of remaining zero inflation. I then conducted the same test for the hurdle model and found that the results were ratioObsSim = 0.99928, p = 1. Since p > .05 again, this meant that there was no statistically significant evidence of remaining zero inflation for the hurdle model either. Because both the ZINB-full and hurdle models passed the DHARMa zero-inflation test, the decision for which model to select is now based on the AIC/BIC comparison of the two model options. The comparison showed that the hurdle model had the lowest AIC (24,330.41) and BIC (24,426.27) of all four models. Thus, I choose to carry forward the hurdle model. 


# Part 6: Testing and probing an interaction

Question: Does the association between the number of chronic conditions and physician visits differ for people based on gender? 

I predict that the association between number of chronic conditions and physician visits differs for male and female patients such that female patients will have a weaker association between the predictor and the outcome variable.  My thinking here is that female health is not well understood in many domains, so while a female patients may be attending many visits to the doctor, they may not be able to report an accurate number of chronic conditions due to the fact that physicians may not provide adequate diagnoses. This would probably be especially true for female patients in the window of time we are examining (1987–1988). 


```{r int-fit}
#| echo: FALSE

# NB model with a chronic x gender interaction.

# chronic * gender expands to chronic + gender + chronic:gender, so both main effects and the product term are included automatically.

# The other predictors (health, school, insurance) are controls.

interact <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ health + school + insurance + chronic * gender,
  data   = data,
  family = nbinom2(link = "log")
)
  
summary(interact)

```

```{r interact lrt}
#| echo: FALSE

# LRT: does adding the chronic x gender interaction improve fit over the additive NB?
lrt_int <- anova(neg_binom, interact)
lrt_int

```

The interaction model did not significantly improve model fit, 
χ²(`r lrt_int[["Chi Df"]][2]`) = 
`r round(lrt_int[["Chisq"]][2], 2)`, 
*p* = `r round(lrt_int[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2], 3)`.

```{r, interact plot}
#| echo: FALSE

# Predicted mean visit counts from the interaction model, on the count scale.
pred_int <- predict_response(interact, terms = c("chronic", "gender"))

int_plot <- plot(pred_int) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(male = "green4", female = "purple")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(male = "green4", female = "purple")) +
  labs(
    title  = "Predicted visit counts by number of chronic conditions and gender",
    x      = "Number of Chronic Conditions", y = "Predicted Visits",
    colour = NULL, fill = NULL
  )

print(int_plot)

```

```{r int-slopes}
#| echo: FALSE

# Simple slopes: the slope of chronic estimated separately within each gender.
slopes <- emtrends(
  interact, 
  specs = ~ gender, 
  var = "chronic")

pairs(slopes)

#test simple slopes against zero
slopes_sum <- summary(slopes, infer = TRUE)
slopes_sum

```

```{r, interac simple-effects}
#| echo: FALSE

chronic_mean <- mean(data$chronic, na.rm = TRUE)
chronic_sd <- sd(data$chronic, na.rm = TRUE)
chronic_values <- chronic_mean + c(-1, 0, 1) * chronic_sd

# Estimated marginal means (EMMs) for each gender at each chronic condition value.
gender_emmeans <- emmeans(
  interact,
  specs = ~ gender | chronic,
  at = list(chronic = chronic_values)
)

# Estimated mean article counts in each gender x chronic condition cell.
summary(gender_emmeans, type = "response")

# Gender differences at each chronic condition value, on the log scale.
pairs(gender_emmeans)

```

The association between chronic conditions and visits is positive and significant for both genders.The p-value of .924 means that the two slopes do not significantly differ. The sign might be flipped because of the order of the subtraction. Since we only have two level for gender. If i called female - male instead, the sign would be positive. The two tests answer the same question with a two-level moderator because there is only one difference between the slopes that we can determine. The emmeans predicted counts differ slightly from the ggeffects plot, and  the contrasts do not because they use different methods, but ultimately the difference remains  the same despite the absolute predictions differing. 

```{r, interaction table}
#| echo: FALSE

contrast_df <- summary(pairs(gender_emmeans)) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  mutate(
    chronic_level = c("-1 SD", "Mean", "+1 SD")[match(round(chronic, 6), round(chronic_values, 6))]
  ) |>
  select(chronic_level, contrast, estimate, SE, z.ratio, p.value)

contrast_df |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    chronic_level = "Chronic conditions", contrast = "Contrast",
    estimate = "Log Contrast", SE = "SE", z.ratio = "z", p.value = "p"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(estimate, SE, z.ratio), decimals = 3) |>
  fmt(columns = p.value,
      fns = \(x) scales::pvalue(x, accuracy = 0.001, add_p = FALSE)) |>
  tab_header(
    title    = "Simple Effects of Gender Across Chronic Conditions",
    subtitle = "Negative-binomial regression (log link)"
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(
    "Log contrasts = Male − Female. z-tests and p-values are computed on the log scale."
  )
```

My hypothesis was not supported. There was no evidence that the association between the number of chronic conditions and physician visits differed between male and female patients. The likelihood-ratio test indicated that adding the chronic conditions × gender interaction did not significantly improve model fit, χ²(1) = 0.009, p = .924.  Chronic conditions were positively associated with physician visits for both males (b = 0.194, p < .001) and females (b = 0.197, p < .001), but the difference between these slopes was not significant (p = .924). Simple-effects comparisons indicated that females had significantly higher predicted physician visit counts than males but, these gender differences did not significantly vary with the number of chronic conditions. So, I am not very confident in this interaction since neither the omnibus nor the probing supported my hypothesis.

7.2. Discussion
What do your results suggest about the relative importance of chronic conditions, self-perceived health, or other variables regarding how often older adults visit a physician? What are the main limitations of this analysis?

example 

Article counts were overdispersed (*M* = 1.69, *s*² = 3.71; 30% zeros). Simulation-based residual checks on a Poisson model showed significant overdispersion (dispersion ratio = 1.99, *p* \< .001) and excess zeros (observed/expected = 1.44, *p* \< .001). A negative binomial model fit significantly better, χ²(1) = 180.20, *p* \< .001, and showed no remaining evidence of overdispersion (ratio = 1.05, *p* = .556) or excess zeros (ratio = 0.99, *p* = .772), so no separate model for zeros was needed.

Holding other predictors constant, women published fewer articles than men (*b* = −0.22, 95% CI \[−0.36, −0.07\], *p* = .003). Each additional child aged 5 or younger was associated with fewer articles (*b* = −0.18, 95% CI \[−0.28, −0.07\], *p* \< .001), and each additional mentor article with more articles (*b* = 0.029, 95% CI \[0.023, 0.035\], *p* \< .001). Marital status (*b* = 0.15, 95% CI \[−0.01, 0.31\], *p* = .067) and PhD prestige (*b* = 0.02, 95% CI \[−0.06, 0.09\], *p* = .672) were not significantly associated with article counts.

Adding a PhD prestige × gender interaction did not significantly improve fit, χ²(1) = 3.73, *p* = .053. Simple slopes showed that prestige was not significantly associated with article counts for men (*b* = −0.04, 95% CI \[−0.14, 0.05\], *p* = .363) or women (*b* = 0.10, 95% CI \[−0.01, 0.20\], *p* = .084). Simple effects, however, showed that the gender gap narrowed as prestige increased. Men were expected to publish more articles than women at low prestige (−1 *SD*; *b* = 0.36, *p* \< .001) and at average prestige (*b* = 0.22, *p* = .002), but the difference was not significant at high prestige (+1 *SD*; *b* = 0.09, *p* = .354).
